items.title: How Do You Know That You Love Somebody? Philosopher Martha Nussbaum’s Incompleteness Theorem of the Heart’s Truth, from Plato to Proust
items.description: "The alternations between love and its denial, suffering and denial of suffering … constitute the most essential and ubiquitous structural feature of the human heart."

items.title: The Dandelion and the Meaning of Life: G.K. Chesterton on How to Live in Wonder
items.description: Recovering the "forgotten blaze or burst of astonishment at our own existence" alive in the back of our modernity-deadened minds.

items.title: C.S. Lewis on How to Structure the Days of a Creative Life and Train the Receptive Imagination
items.description: There are, in my experience, two fundaments of the creative life: putting yourself regularly in the path of wonder and getting out of your own way in order to receive what you encounter there. Wonder, like enchantment, is not something you can control or plan for or will — it is something that befalls you, overcomes you, pours upon you spontaneous and unbidden. items.title: Orcas and the Price of Consciousness: Lessons in Love and Loss from Earth’s Most Successful and Creative Predator
items.description: Marbling the waters of every ocean with their billows of black and white, orcas are Earth’s most creative and most successful apex predator. Although they are known as killer whales, they are the largest member of the dolphin family. Older than great white sharks, they hunt everything from seals a tenth their size to moose bathing in the shallows to Earth’s largest animal — the blue whale, whose tongue alone can weigh as much as a female orca. items.title: Ocean of Stars: A Painted Poem About How to Bear the Astonishment of Life
items.description: Here we are, bewildered miracles of chemistry and chance, trembling embers of dead stars capable of sign and song, a wild bet against probability that won. We have dreamt up origin myths and cosmological models, built the Taj Mahal and the Large Hadron Collider, to fathom where we came from and where we are going. items.title: Dostoyevsky on What Makes a Good Person
items.description: We know good people when we encounter them, when they fall upon our lives like a sunbeam, like a song. But we don’t always know what makes them good. It has, of course, a lot to do with kindness. It has to do with their capacity to give, and also to receive. It has to do with their courage of uncertainty. items.title: Inner Space, Outer Space, and How to Be an Astronaut in the Cosmos of Connection: Eric Berne on the Key to True Intimacy
items.description: "A star is the glowing light inside the other person, distantly seen, brave soul’s tiny flame, too bright to approach without great courage and integrity."

items.title: What Happens When We Die
items.description: "How can a creature who will certainly die have an understanding of things that will exist forever?"

items.title: How to Say “YES” to Life
items.description: It started with an urn for living gone wrong, the clay kiltering off center, resisting my every effort to force it back into shape. The harder I pushed to control it, the more it took on a life of its own, folding like flesh, bending like mind. I pushed and despaired, pushed and despaired, until, exhausted and exasperated, I gave up and simply let my hands follow the momentum of the clay, saying “YES” to its will. items.title: David Bowie Answers the Famous Proust Questionnaire
items.description: "Q: What do you regard as the lowest depth of misery? A: Living in fear."

items.title: Bertrand Russell on the Secret of Happiness
items.description: "Let your interests be as wide as possible, and let your reactions to the things and persons that interest you be as far as possible friendly rather than hostile."

items.title: Richard Dawkins on the Luckiness of Death
items.description: "The potential people who could have been here in my place but who will in fact never see the light of day outnumber the sand grains of Arabia."

items.title: James Baldwin’s Advice on Writing
items.description: "Talent is insignificant. I know a lot of talented ruins. Beyond talent lie all the usual words: discipline, love, luck, but most of all, endurance."

items.title: Against Brute Force: D.H. Lawrence on the Superpower of Vulnerability
items.description: "Brute force crushes many plants. Yet the plants rise again. The Pyramids will not last a moment compared with the daisy."

items.title: The Common Language of Science: Einstein’s Clarion Call to Divided Humanity in a Rare 1941 Recording
items.description: “Perfection of means and confusion of goals seem — in my opinion — to characterize our age.”
